parts:
Hello all,
I am really hoping to receive some clarification on the goodness-of-fit procedure for single season occupancy. 

I have looked through many of the posts found within this group, and read through some of the literature that had details on gof in the methods, but I am still a bit confused. I believe I have 3 options: 

1) the chi squared (Fiske and Chandler 2011) 
2) Freeman-Tukey (Sillet et al. 2012)
3) mb.gof.test (Mackenzie and Bailey)

Each obviously give different results, very different. Below is the code I have used to do these 3 gof tests. I have also attached the outputted histogram for each as well. 

# Chi and Freeman
fitstats <- function(Mod) {
  observed <- getY(Mod@data)
  expected <- fitted(Mod)
  resids <- residuals(Mod)
  sse <- sum(resids^2,na.rm=TRUE)
  chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected,na.rm=TRUE)
  freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2,na.rm=TRUE)
  out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)
  return(out)
}
pb <- parboot(oc4, fitstats, nsim=100, report=1)
pb

Looking at the results
1) the chi squared (Fiske and Chandler 2011) 
p-value = 0.990, c-hat = 0.95
Histogram: The observed statistic lies on the very far left, outside of the bootstrap values.

2) Freeman-Tukey (Sillet et al. 2012)
p-value = 0.832, c-hat = 0.99
Histogram: Looks great. the observed statistic lies within the bulk of the bootstrap values.

3) mb.gof.test (Mackenzie and Bailey)
p-value = 0, c-hat = 27.34 
Histogram: The observed statistic lie on the very far right, outside of the bootstrap values.


I've read that for a good fit model, the observed statistic should lie within the bulk of the bootstrapped values. This is the case for the Freeman-tukeys, but not so for either chi-squared or the Mackenzie Bailey methods. Both the chi-squared and freeman methods have c-hat values very close to 1, whereas the mb.gof.test is 27! Perhaps something isn't working quite right behind the scenes for the mb.gof.test with my model?

I'm no statistician, but I am trying to learn as I go. Please let me know if I am making some fatal error, or doing something entirely inappropriate here.

I'm just not sure what the next best step would be for me given all of the above. Any insight or suggestions on how to approach this problem is very much appreciated. 

Thank you all,

parts:
The number of bootstrap samples is too small; nsim = 100 or 5.  

nsim

the number of bootstrap samples. The recommended number of samples varies with the data set, but should be on the order of 1000 or 5000, and in cases with a large number of visits, even 10 000 samples, namely to reduce the effect of unusually small values of the test statistics.

Best,

Matt

messages.author: 4e956cc50ac3e075
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Goodness of fit question - selecting, implementing, and interpreting
parts:
Hi Paul,

if you have occupancy data, you need to summarize the information in
some way (e.g., frequencies with detection histories as in the
MacKenzie and Bailey test). It is not appropriate to do a chi-square
test on raw binary data (see McCullagh and Nelder 1989: Generalized
linear models, 2nd edition. Chapman and Hall.). Also, you need more
samples to check GOF (e.g., 1000, 5000, or 10000): 5 is definitely not
enough for the MacKenzie and Bailey test.

Hope it helps,

Marc
--

parts:
Hi Paul,

you can do a Chisquare test to serve as GoF test statistic for an occupancy model all right, but the key thing is: on what data ? You cannot do it directly on the binary detection histories, because binary data are uninformative about lack of fit. So if anybody runs a Chisquare on them as a way of testing GoF, then this is wrong (and I have done so myself, even published....). What one has to do is to aggregate the binary data such that you get some sort of counts statistic (i.e., with numbers greater than 1 also). The MB test is exactly one way of doing such an aggregation. Then, running a Chisquare on the frequencies of the detection histories is OK.

Best regards  --- (The other) Marc

On Tuesday, September 18, 2018 at 11:01:17 AM UTC-5, Marc Mazerolle wrote:
Hi Paul,

if you have occupancy data, you need to summarize the information in
some way (e.g., frequencies with detection histories as in the
MacKenzie and Bailey test). It is not appropriate to do a chi-square
test on raw binary data (see McCullagh and Nelder 1989: Generalized
linear models, 2nd edition. Chapman and Hall.). Also, you need more
samples to check GOF (e.g., 1000, 5000, or 10000): 5 is definitely not
enough for the MacKenzie and Bailey test.

Hope it helps,

Marc

Each obviously give different results, very different. Below is the code I have used to do these 3 gof tests. I have also attached the outputted histogram for each as well. 

# Chi and Freeman
fitstats <- function(Mod) {
  observed <- getY(Mod@data)
  expected <- fitted(Mod)
  resids <- residuals(Mod)
  sse <- sum(resids^2,na.rm=TRUE)
  chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected,na.rm=TRUE)
  freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2,na.rm=TRUE)
  out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)
  return(out)
}
